Synergistic enhancement of methane yield and odor control in pig manure 
anaerobic digestion via micro-aeration pretreatment

Microbial community structure
A B S T R A C T
The widespread adoption of anaerobic digestion for pig manure treatment is limited by malodorous gas emissions 
and low energy recovery efficiency. This study systematically examined the effects of micro-aeration pretreat­
ment over a range of intensities (0-13.9 mL/g(TS)/d) on odor abatement and digestion performance. Micro- 
aeration reduced emissions of eight key malodorous gases, including sulfide (H2S), ammonia (NH3), meth­
anethiol (CH4S), and ethanethiol (C2H6S), by 14.0-100%. Complete sulfide mineralization was achieved at in­
tensities ≥9.3 mL/g(TS)/d. Mitigation of nitrogen- and sulfur-containing compounds was likely driven by 
selective enrichment of facultative aerobic consortia (e.g., unclassified_f__Bacillaceae and unclassi­
fied_c__Gammaproteobacteria) and the upregulation of sulfur oxidation and nitrogen transformation pathways. 
Methane production increased by 37.6-95.5%, owing to enhanced hydrolysis and acetogenesis resulting from 
upregulated fatty acid β-oxidation and acetyl-CoA synthesis. Moreover, syntrophic bacteria (Syntrophomonas) 
and key methanogens (Methanothrix and Methanosarcina) were selectively enriched. An aeration intensity of 
4.6 mL/g(TS)/d was identified as optimal, as it balanced effective odor control and maximal methanogenic 
activity. These findings provide a theoretical foundation and a viable strategy for improving energy recovery and 
environmental sustainability in swine manure management.
1. Introduction
The rapid expansion of the global pig industry has led to a severe 
accumulation of manure, presenting a severe environmental manage­
ment challenge [1]. Consequently, developing efficient treatment and 
resource recovery strategies for pig manure is essential for environ­
mental protection and sustainable agricultural development [2]. 
Although rich in organic matter and nutrients, pig manure is charac­
terized by an imbalanced carbon-to-nitrogen ratio [3]. Its improper 
disposal poses significant environmental risks, such as water eutrophi­
cation, soil contamination with heavy metals, and atmospheric pollution 
[4]. Among these concerns, the emission of intense and complex 
malodorous gases during microbial degradation represents one of the 
most immediate and perceptible hazards [5]. The emission of these 
malodorous gases not only creates a public nuisance and restricts the 
siting of farming and processing facilities, but also poses health risks to 
onsite workers [6].
Anaerobic digestion (AD) has been widely recognized as a promising 
technology for treating pig manure, achieving simultaneous stabiliza­
tion, volume reduction, and energy recovery in the form of methane 
(CH4) [7]. Nevertheless, the traditional anaerobic digestion process is 
often plagued by inherent limitations, such as low CH4 yield and the 
persistent release of substantial amounts of malodorous gases [8,9]. 
Sulfur and nitrogen-containing compounds are key contributors to these 
foul-smelling gases [10,11]. These compounds are formed due to the 
incomplete microbial degradation of sulfur-containing amino acids and 
nitrogen-rich organic matter in pig manure under anaerobic conditions 
[12]. These malodorous gases not only impeded the broader adoption of 
AD technology but also compromises the safe handling and utilization of 
its by-products [13].

The micro-aeration pretreatment has gained significant attention as 
an economically viable method for controlling malodorous gases at the 
source [14]. The core principle involves creating a micro-aerobic envi­
ronment through controlled oxygen introduction, thereby directly sup­
pressing obligate anaerobic odor-producing bacteria, such as 
sulfate-reducing bacteria [15]. In such an environment, facultative 
and aerobic bacteria are promoted to oxidize odorous precursors into 
odorless or low-odor substances [16]. Concurrently, this approach can 
regulate nitrogen conversion and mitigate ammonia volatilization [17]. 
For example, microorganisms can facilitate the simultaneous trans­
formation and removal of nitrogenous and sulfurous malodorous gases 
by converting ammonia (NH3) to nitrate and oxidizing volatile sulfur 
compounds to sulfate [18,19]. However, during the process of 
micro-aeration pretreatment, a large number of aerobic or facultative 
aerobic microorganisms are enriched in the aerobic environment, which 
maybe not suitable for anaerobic fermentation system [20]. While ox­
ygen can suppress the formation of malodorous compounds, it also ox­
idizes labile organic carbon to CO2, resulting in irreversible carbon loss 
and a potential reduction in methane yield [15]. Furthermore, current 
odor evaluation systems remain incomplete. Most studies predomi­
nantly focus on H2S and NH3, while neglecting other significant 
malodorous compounds such as trimethylamine (C3H9N), methanethiol 
(CH4S), ethanethiol (C2H6S), dimethyl disulfide (C2H6S2), and carbon 
disulfide (CS2). Additionally, few studies have systematically quantified, 
within a unified framework, the relationship between aeration intensity, 
organic matter loss, and terminal methane production. Therefore, the 
effects of micro-aeration treatment on malodorous gases control, 
organic matter loss, and methane production urgently require 
examination.
Most existing studies only analyze H2S and NH3 emissions and 
overlook critical odorants including trimethylamine, methanethiol, 
ethanethiol, dimethyl disulfide and carbon disulfide. Furthermore, no 
unified experimental system has yet quantified the coupled interplay of 
aeration intensity, organic matter mineralization and final methane 
output. Collectively, the scarcity of research in these areas demonstrates 
an urgent need to clarify how micro-aeration simultaneously regulates 
odor release, carbon loss, and methanogenic performance.
Given the aforementioned challenges, this study aims to (1) sys­
tematically quantify the release of key malodorous gases (NH3, C3H9N, 
H2S, CH4S, C2H6S, C2H6S2, CS2) and overall odor levels under seven 
micro-aeration intensities (0-13.9 mL/g(TS)/d; (2) evaluate the long- 
term anaerobic digestion performance of pretreated manure and estab­
lish a quantitative relationship among aeration intensity, carbon loss, 
and CH4 yield; and (3) elucidate how aeration intensity drives microbial 
community dynamics, including diversity, assembly processes, keystone 
taxa, and functional potential. These findings will provide an integrated 
scientific basis for the precise optimization of micro-aeration pretreat­
ment in pig manure AD.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Raw materials and pretreatment
Fresh pig manure was obtained from a large-scale farm in Xiuwen 
County, Guiyang, Guizhou Province, and promptly stored at 4 ± 1 ◦C. 
The basic physicochemical properties of the raw manure are summa­
rized in Table S1.
2.2. Micro-aeration pretreatment system
The micro-aeration pretreatment system is provided in Fig. S1. Pig 
manure with a total solids (TS) content of 22.5% was subjected to static 
micro-aeration for 20 days. Seven aeration intensity gradients were 
applied: 0 (control), 2.3, 3.5, 4.6, 5.8, 9.3, and 13.9 mL/g(TS)/d, each in 
triplicate. During pretreatment, samples were collected every 5 days (0, 
5, 10, 15, and 20 days) for analysis. Dissolved oxygen (DO), oxidation- 
reduction potential (ORP), pH, and electrical conductivity (EC) of the 
fermentation slurry were monitored in situ using a HQ40d portable 
analyzer (HACH, USA), while gas samples were collected for subsequent 
analysis.
2.3. Sequential batch AD system
Sequential batch AD was presented in Fig. S2. Pig manure pretreated 
for 20 days at three aeration intensities (0, 4.6, and 13.9 mL/g(TS)/d) 
was used as the substrate for AD assessment. For each treatment, the 
total solids concentration was adjusted to 10%, maintaining a working 
volume of 150 mL per bottle. Digestion was conducted at 35 ± 1 ◦C 
under anaerobic conditions for 48 days. Before incubation, each bottle 
was purged with high-purity nitrogen for 2 min to remove residual ox­
ygen and ensure obligate anaerobiosis. Biogas was collected in Tedlar 
gas bags (DuPont, USA), which were equipped with two valves (one for 
inlet, one for sampling). At 24 h intervals, the gas volume was measured 
with a gas-tight syringe via the sampling valve. After measurement, the 
bag was evacuated and reconnected to the bottle. Gas volumes were 
normalized to standard temperature and pressure (0 ◦C, 1 atm). All 
experiments were carried out in triplicate.
2.4. Analytical methods
CH4 was quantified using a GC-1120 gas chromatograph (GC, 
Shanghai, China) equipped with a thermal conductivity detector (TCD) 
and a Porapak Q packed column (2 mm × 3 mm i.d.). High-purity N2 
(99.999%) served as the carrier gas at a flow rate of 30 mL/min. The 
injector, column oven, and detector temperatures were set to 100 ◦C, 
80 ◦C, and 150 ◦C, respectively. Sulfur-containing malodorous gases, 
including H2S, CH4S, C2H6S, C2H6S2, and CS2, were measured on the 
same GC system equipped with a flame photometric detector (FPD).

2.5. Microbial community analysis
Fresh pig manure without pretreatment (CK group) and manure 
pretreated at aeration intensities of 0 (A0 group), 4.6 (A4.6 group), and 
13.9 mL/g(TS)/d (A13.9 group) for 20 days were subjected to 16S rRNA 
high-throughput sequencing (Meiji Biomedical Technology Co., Ltd., 
China). Total genomic DNA was extracted using the FastDNA Spin Kit for 
Soil (MP Biomedicals, USA) and assessed for quality via 1% agarose gel 
electrophoresis. The V3-V4 region of the bacterial 16S rRNA gene was 
amplified in triplicate with primers 341F/806R and TransStart FastPfu 
DNA polymerase on an ABI GeneAmp 9700 PCR System (Applied Bio­
systems, USA). Amplified products were pooled, purified, and quantified 
(CFX Connect&T100, Bio-Rad System, USA) before library construction 
using the TruSeq DNA PCR-Free Kit (Illumina, USA). Sequencing was 
performed on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform.
Raw reads were processed through Fastp (v0.23.4) and FLASH 
(v1.2.11) for quality control and assembly. Amplicon sequence variants 
(ASVs) were generated using DADA2 in QIIME2 (v2024.5) and taxo­
nomically annotated against the SILVA database (v138). Microbial di­
versity (α- and β-diversity), community structure, and biomarker 
identification (LEfSe) were analyzed with QIIME2 and R packages 
(vegan, ggplot2). Functional prediction of metabolic pathways was 
performed with PICRUSt2 based on KEGG orthology. All bioinformatics 
analyses were conducted on the Majorbio Cloud Platform (www.maj 
orbio.com).
2.6. Statistical analysis
All experimental data were processed initially in Microsoft Excel 
2019. Analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed using SPSS soft­
ware, with post-hoc multiple comparisons conducted via Duncan's test 
at a significance level of p < 0.05. Key Figures were prepared using 
Origin 2024 software.
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Malodorous gases production
3.1.1. Nitrogen containing gases
The effects of different aeration intensities on malodorous gases 
production during AD are shown in Figs. 1 and 2. Fig. 1A illustrated the 
influence of aeration intensity on NH3 release. Except for the 3.5 mL/g 
(TS)/d treatment, which exhibited a slightly higher NH3 concentration 
than the unaerated control (0 mL/g(TS)/d) on day 5. All aerated treat­
ments produced significantly lower NH3 levels throughout the 20-day 
incubation period. This observation is consistent with previous studies 
demonstrating that low oxygen concentrations can markedly inhibit 
NH3 generation [21]. In all aeration groups, NH3 was undetectable until 
day 20. Higher aeration intensities (9.3 and 13.9 mL/g(TS)/d) notably 
shortened the NH3 release period by 5 and 10 days, respectively. 
Compared with the control, NH3 production on day 10 was reduced by 
63.2%, 65.8%, 58.7%, 64.9%, 83.4%, and 96.8% in the 2.3, 3.5, 4.6, 5.8, 
9.3, and 13.9 mL/g(TS)/d groups, respectively. This significant reduc­
tion in NH3 emissions is primarily attributed to the oxygen introduced 
during aeration, which promotes the activity of aerobic nitrifying bac­
teria [22]. These microorganisms oxidize ammonium to nitrate via 
nitrification and partially assimilate NH4
+ into biomass, thereby funda­
mentally mitigating the accumulation and volatilization of NH3 [23]. 
However, digestate contains relatively high levels of inorganic nitrogen 
[17]. Direct application of this digestate to agricultural land may lead to 
soluble nitrogen being transported via surface runoff into water bodies, 
triggering eutrophication [24]. Therefore, it is recommended to (1) 
apply digestate at quantity matched to crop nitrogen demand, (2) 
recover nitrogen from digestate through pretreatment, (3) combine 
digestate with straw to balance the C/N ratio and enhance microbial 
nitrogen transformation, and (4) establish field buffer strips to absorb 
excess nitrogen [25]. These measures can effectively prevent excessive 
soluble nitrogen in digestate from entering water bodies and causing 
eutrophication.

day 20, C3H9N yields in treatment groups with aeration intensities 
≥4.6 mL/g(TS)/d were consistently lower than those in the control 
group. On day 10, C3H9N production in the 4.6, 5.8, 9.3, and 13.9 mL/g

3.1.2. Sulfur-containing gases
With prolonged pretreatment time, H2S production in all treatment 
groups exhibited a declining trend (Fig. 1C). Notably, during days 5-20, 
H2S levels in groups with aeration intensities ≥4.6 mL/g(TS)/d were 
significantly lower than those in the non-aerated control. By day 20, all 
aerated groups showed reduced H2S production relative to the control. 
On day 15, H2S emissions decreased by 40.0%, 66.7%, 84.5%, 77.8%, 
100%, and 100% in the 2.3, 3.5, 4.6, 5.8, 9.3, and 13.9 mL/g(TS)/ 
d groups, respectively, compared to the control. These results confirm 
that aeration pretreatment effectively suppresses H2S generation during 
subsequent anaerobic treatment of pig manure. H2S is primarily pro­
duced by obligate anaerobic sulfate-reducing bacteria (SRB), which 
utilize sulfate as an electron acceptor under anaerobic conditions [28]. 
Oxygen introduced during aeration strongly inhibited the metabolic 
activity of SRB and enriched sulfur-oxidizing bacteria (SOB), which 
might be one of the key reasons for the reduction of H2S [29]. However, 
during the early pretreatment phase (5 and 10 days), H2S production in 
the low-intensity aeration groups (2.3 and 3.5 mL/g(TS)/d) exceeded 
that of the control. This may be attributed to weak aeration stimulating 
aerobic or facultatively anaerobic microorganisms to decompose com­
plex sulfur-containing organics into simpler reduced sulfur compounds, 
which are more readily utilized by SRB [30]. Although SRB activity is 
partially inhibited, increased substrate availability could temporarily 
promote H2S production [31]. No H2S was detected in the high-intensity 
aeration groups (9.3 and 13.9 mL/g(TS)/d) after day 15, indicating that 
higher aeration not only reduced H2S formation but also completely 
halted its release.
CH4S production was significantly inhibited in all aeration treatment 
groups, with the inhibition degree positively correlated with aeration 
intensity (Fig. 1D). On day 5, CH4S concentrations decreased by 37.0% 
in the 4.6 mL/g(TS)/d group and by 47.0% in the 13.9 mL/g(TS)/ 
d group compared to the control. By day 10, CH4S levels in aerated 
groups ranged from 13.0% to 76.1% of the control, with reductions to 
25.8% and 23.9% observed in the 4.6 and 13.9 mL/g(TS)/d groups, 
respectively. Complete elimination of CH4S was achieved by day 20 in 
the 9.3 and 13.9 mL/g(TS)/d treatments. These results indicate that 
aeration pretreatment accelerates the conversion and removal of CH4S, 
with complete inhibition achieved at an intensity threshold of ≥9.3 mL/ 
g(TS)/d. This effect may be attributed to the enrichment of facultative 
and aerobic microorganisms, which oxidize CH4S to odorless dimethyl 
disulfide or further mineralize it to sulfate within local micro-aerobic 
micro-niches formed during micro-aeration pretreatment [4].
The variation patterns of C2H6S and C2H6S2 are presented in Fig. 1E 
and F. C2H6S, an important oxidation product of C2H6S2, belongs to the 
chemical class of sulfur-containing organic compounds [32]. In the 
non-aerated control, both compounds persisted until day 20, while 
aeration significantly enhanced their removal. Notably, at a moderate 
aeration intensity of 2.3 mL/g(TS)/d on day 10, an 80.6% decrease in 
C2H6S2 concentration was accompanied by a 45.2% increase in C2H6S, 
directly confirming the aerobic conversion of C2H6S2 to C2H6S in the 
system. When aeration intensity reached ≥9.3 mL/g(TS)/d, both sul­
fides were simultaneously and completely removed by day 15. These 
results indicate that low-intensity aeration primarily regulates odor 
through structural transformation (malodorous thiol → malodorous di­
sulfide), whereas high-intensity aeration achieves odor elimination via 
complete mineralization (sulfide → sulfate). The effective odor eradi­
cation under high aeration may be attributed to the enrichment of

CS2 removal exhibited distinct responses to aeration intensity

On day 5, CS2 levels decreased by 41.3% and 42.6% in the 4.6 and 
13.9 mL/g(TS)/d groups, respectively, compared to the control. Mod­

zero between days 15-20. Notably, the threshold for complete CS2 
removal (4.6 mL/g(TS)/d) was lower than that required for complete 
mineralization of C2H6S and C2H6S2 (≥9.3 mL/g(TS)/d), suggesting that 
CS2 may be more susceptible to oxidative degradation [34]. This dif­
ferential sensitivity highlights the potential for implementing tiered 
control strategies targeting specific malodorous sulfides.
3.1.3. Integrated odor assessment
Odor pollution is a widespread environmental issue with a subjective 
nature. Trace sulfur- and nitrogen-containing volatiles can trigger 
discomfort and complaints [18]. In the European Union (EU), odor 
emissions from livestock and anaerobic digestion are regulated under 
the Industrial Emissions Directive (2010/75/EU) via site permits and 
best available techniques [35]. Odor was quantified by dynamic olfac­
tometry (EN 13725) and expressed in ouE/m3, where 1 ouE/m3 is 
defined as the dilution-to-threshold ratio at the human perception 
threshold. Residential/rural limits are 5-10 ouE/m3 [12]. Thus, odor 
removal evaluation requires whole-sample holistic assessment, not just 
individual compound quantification.
Changes in overall odor concentration are presented in Fig. 2B. 
Initial variations may be attributed to the physical stripping effect 
induced by higher aeration intensities. After system stabilization on day 
5, the lowest odor concentration was observed in the 13.9 mL/g(TS)/ 
d treatment. Notably, odor concentration did not exhibit a simple linear 
decrease with increasing aeration intensity. Instead, the low-intensity 
groups (2.3-4.6 mL/g(TS)/d) displayed lower odor levels than the 
moderate-intensity groups (5.8 and 9.3 mL/g(TS)/d) after day 5, sug­
gesting that suboptimal aeration may exacerbate odor formation. 
Although major odorants (H2S, NH3, C3H9N) were suppressed in aerated 
groups, overall odor is influenced by a mixture of compounds such as 
phenols, aldehydes, and intermediate sulfides [36]. Moderate aeration 
may therefore facilitate the accumulation of certain non-target 
malodorous intermediates. Based on integrated odor and key gas re­
sults, aeration intensities of 4.6 and 13.9 mL/g(TS)/d demonstrated 
relatively better overall odor reduction.
3.1.4. Methane production during micro-aeration pretreatment
CH4 production during micro-aeration pretreatment is shown in 
Fig. 2C. At the onset of pretreatment (day 0), CH4 yields in several 
aerated groups (3.5, 5.8, 9.3, and 13.9 mL/g(TS)/d) were slightly higher 
than in the non-aerated control. This transient increase may be attrib­
uted to improved mass transfer or suppression of competing microbial 
groups such as sulfate-reducing bacteria [37]. However, as pretreatment 
progressed, the inhibitory effect of aeration became predominant. A 
critical threshold was observed at 4.6 mL/g(TS)/d, with CH4 production 
decreasing by 71.7% relative to the initial value by day 5, indicating 
substantial compression of anaerobic niches. At higher intensities (9.3 
and 13.9 mL/g(TS)/d), methanogenesis was completely inhibited, and 
no CH4 was detected after day 15, reflecting a systemic metabolic shift 
toward aerobic/facultative oxidative pathways.
These dynamics illustrate the gradient inhibitory effect of oxygen on 
obligate anaerobic metabolism. The synchronous reduction in CH4 and 
malodorous gases reveals an aeration-driven transition from anaerobic 
fermentation producing reduced end-products such as CH4 and H2S, to 
aerobic/facultative oxidation, yielding oxidized products including CO2 
and sulfate [38].
3.2. Organic matter characteristics and physicochemical properties of pig 
manure
3.2.1. Dry matter loss
The temporal variation in dry matter mass and the final loss rates 
under different aeration intensities are shown in Fig. 2D. The initial dry 
matter mass was 1005.09 ± 4.10 g. After 20 days of pretreatment, all 
treatment groups exhibited dry matter loss. The unaerated control group 
showed a natural loss rate of 19.0%. Aeration significantly increased this 
loss, with rates positively correlated with aeration intensity, loss rates 
were 24.5%, 23.9%, 28.9%, 34.0%, 36.2%, and 38.8% for the 2.3, 3.5, 
4.6, 5.8, 9.3, and 13.9 mL/g(TS)/d groups, respectively. In the highest- 
intensity group (13.9 mL/g(TS)/d), only 615.33 g of dry matter 
remained. This dry matter loss mainly results from the aerobic miner­
alization of labile organic carbon to CO2 [39]. Moreover, the progressive 
mass loss observed with increasing aeration intensity indicated that 
oxygen supplementation promotes carbon mineralization to CO2. These 
results clearly indicate that aeration pretreatment accelerates the aero­
bic mineralization and depletion of organic matter, which may reduce 
the total substrate available for subsequent anaerobic methanogenesis.
3.2.2. Dynamics of physicochemical parameters
DO variations are presented in Fig. 3A. The DO level in the system 
was not a simple linear function of aeration intensity but resulted from 
the dynamic balance between microbial oxygen consumption and 
physical oxygen supply, indirectly reflecting microbial metabolic ac­
tivity [37]. In the unaerated control group, DO continuously declined 
due to microbial consumption and was nearly depleted by day 20. In 
aerated groups with intensities ≥4.6 mL/g(TS)/d, DO increased rapidly 
after day 5 and remained elevated, indicating sufficient oxygen supply 
to support vigorous metabolism by aerobic and facultatively anaerobic 
microorganisms. Conversely, in low-intensity groups (2.3 and 3.5 mL/g 
(TS)/d), DO rose slowly and began to decrease after days 15 and 10, 
respectively, suggesting that the oxygen supply rate was insufficient to 
meet microbial demand, thereby limiting aerobic processes such as 
nitrification and sulfur oxidation. Previous studies have reported that 
obligate anaerobes require anoxic conditions (DO < 0.1 mg/L), facul­
tative anaerobes grow in the micro-aerobic range (DO concentration was 
0.1-0.5 mg/L), and aerobes/facultative microbes thrive under aerobic 
conditions (DO > 0.5 mg/L) [40]. In this study, during zero-aeration 
pretreatment, DO dropped from 0.2 mg/L to 0, supporting the growth 
of both facultative and obligate anaerobes. At aeration intensities of 
2.3-3.5 mL/g(TS)/d, DO ranged from 0.1 to 0.4 mg/L, providing 
micro-aerobic conditions conducive to facultative anaerobes. At aera­
tion intensities ≥4.6 mL/g(TS)/d, DO exceeded 0.5 mg/L, creating 
aerobic conditions that favored aerobes and facultative microbes and 
potentially inhibited the growth of obligate anaerobes. These findings 
explain, from a DO availability perspective, why aeration intensities 
≥4.6 mL/g(TS)/d achieve faster and more effective suppression of 
malodorous gas generation.
The ORP changes are shown in Fig. 3B. ORP serves as an electro­
chemical indicator of the oxidative or reductive capacity within a 
fermentation system [41]. In the unaerated control group, ORP 
decreased to −288.53 mV by day 20, reflecting a strongly reducing 
environment conducive to obligate anaerobes. In contrast, ORP in all 
aerated groups remained between −152.80 and −85.20 mV, a range 
more favorable for facultative anaerobes and certain anaerobic micro­
organisms. The elevated ORP indicates a metabolic shift from obligate 
anaerobic to facultative/micro-aerobic conditions. This change directly 
influences microbial community structure and represents a key envi­
ronmental driver in redirecting odor-related metabolic pathways [42].

accumulation of volatile fatty acids (VFAs) from organic matter hydro­

3.3. Methane production during anaerobic digestion
The CH4 production from pig manure during 50-day AD following 
different pretreatments is shown in Fig. 3E. Daily CH4 profiles of all 
treatment groups exhibited typical digestion phases: lag, rising, and 
declining. Notably, although the unaerated pretreatment group (A0) 
(454.4 mL/g VS) showed higher cumulative CH4 production, likely due 
to its lower ORP promoting early methanogen colonization, untreated 
raw manure (CK) yielded the lowest cumulative CH4 output (232.4 mL/ 
g VS). This suggests that pretreatment modifies substrate characteristics 
through initial microbial metabolism, thereby enhancing subsequent AD 
performance [43]. However, cumulative CH4 production from manure 
pretreated at 4.6 (351.0 mL/g VS) and 13.9 mL/g(TS)/d (319.7 mL/g 
VS) were lower than those of the unaerated pretreatment group (A0). 
This contrasts with several reports indicating that in situ micro-aeration 
enhances CH4 yield [44]. In this study, AD was conducted in sequential 
batch mode following pretreatment. High-intensity aeration induced 
substantial organic matter mineralization during pretreatment (dry 
matter loss up to 38.8%) and elevated the initial ORP of the substrate 
upon entry into the anaerobic reactor. Together, these factors reduced 
the total carbon available for methanogenesis and slowed anaerobic 
startup [45]. Therefore, although aeration may optimize microbial 
functionality, irreversible carbon loss emerges as the dominant 
constraint on overall CH4 production.
An aeration intensity of 4.6 mL/g(TS)/d exhibited the relatively 
optimal balance between malodorous gases reduction and energy re­
covery. The maximum daily gas production rate and cumulative CH4 
yield achieved at this intensity were significantly higher than those from 
the 13.9 mL/g(TS)/d pretreatment and from untreated raw manure 
(CK). Although its cumulative CH4 output was slightly lower than that of 
the unaerated pretreatment group (A0), it simultaneously delivered 
substantial malodorous gases mitigation. These results underscore the 
inherent challenge of simultaneously maximizing malodorous gases 
control and CH4 recovery within a single process. Thus, 4.6 mL/g(TS)/ 
d can be regarded as an optimal operational point, effectively control­
ling malodorous gases while retaining high methanogenic potential 
within an acceptable range of carbon loss. Excessively high aeration 
intensities, such as 13.9 mL/g(TS)/d, are economically inefficient unless 
complete malodorous gases elimination is the sole and absolute objec­
tive. Furthermore, micro-aeration pretreatment outperforms the co- 
digestion of carbon-rich substrates by eliminating the need for 
external carbon sources, enabling real-time flexible control, enhancing 
methane production, and reducing emissions of malodorous gases [46]. 
However, micro-aeration pretreatment does not modify the overall C/N 
ratio and demands stringent aeration control to prevent the suppression 
of methane production. Nevertheless, micro-aeration pretreatment is 
particularly advantageous for intensive pig farms that lack accessible 
crop residues or other carbon-rich wastes.
3.4. Microbial community structure and diversity
3.4.1. α- and β-diversity
High-throughput sequencing was employed to analyze micro- 
aeration-induced shifts in microbial community, thereby revealing the 
mechanisms for odor release and methane production. The Coverage 
index exceeded 0.999 for all samples, confirming that sequencing depth 
was sufficient to represent the true community composition. As shown in 
Table S2, species richness indices (ACE, Chao1, and Sobs) followed the 
order A13.9 > A4.6 > A0 > CK, indicating that aeration pretreatment, 
especially at higher intensities, significantly expanded the microbial 
species pool. However, group A4.6 exhibited the highest Shannon index, 
reflecting greater community evenness and integrated diversity. Simi­
larly, the Simpson index was significantly higher in groups A0 and A4.6 
than in CK and A13.9 (Fig. S3). These results suggest that moderate 
aeration (4.6 mL/g(TS)/d) promoted a more evenly distributed and 
structurally stable community, which may correlate with its optimized 
system performance.

3.6. Integrated microbial assembly and functional adaptation under 
micro-aeration
Micro-aeration pretreatment systematically restructured microbial 
community assembly and functional interaction networks (See 
supplementary material Text 1-5). Specifically, infer phylogenetic-bin- 
based null model (iCAMP) analysis revealed that moderate aeration 
(4.6 mL/g(TS)/d) maximized stochastic drift (61.5%) and community 
stability (Fig. 4E–F). In contrast, high aeration re-imposed selective 
pressure, leading to functional simplification (Fig. 6C–D). Moreover, 
compared with the CK group, generalist species dominated all groups 
(>80%) after aeration at 4.6 mL/g(TS)/d, while the proportion of 
neutral species decreased from 6.6% to below 3.5%, enhancing com­
munity stability and functional efficiency (Fig. S8). Key taxa succession 
was traced from fermentative (CK) to syntrophic (A0/A4.6) and ulti­
mately to methanogenic communities (A13.9) using linear discriminant 
analysis effect size (LEfSe) analysis (Fig. S9A–S9B). Statistical analysis 
revealed 338 genera exhibiting significant abundance differences 
(p < 0.01, Fig. S9), with a higher degree of compositional similarity 
between A0 and A4.6 (Fig. S10). After aeration pretreatment, Meth­
anosarcina and Methanothrix established a cooperative network, with 
Methanothrix accounting for 20% relative abundance in A4.6. This 
network reduced odor precursor and maintained methanogenic func­
tional redundancy [37].
PICRUSt2-based functional prediction revealed up-regulation of 
sulfur oxidation, sulfate reduction, nitrogen fixation, and C1 compound 
degradation in group A4.6 compared with the CK group. These func­
tional enhancements contributed to effective odorant removal [38]. In 
the A4.6 group, carbon flux was redirected and enhanced via fatty acid 
β-oxidation, the TCA cycle, and acetyl-CoA synthesis. These metabolic 
shifts facilitated volatile fatty acid degradation and augmented the 
availability of methanogenic substrates [43]. This functional synergy 
enabled at aeration of 4.6 mL/g(TS)/d to achieve optimal odor control 
and methane production.
4. Conclusions
Micro-aeration reduced the concentrations of the eight target odor­
ants (NH3, C3H9N, H2S, CH4S, C2H6S, C2H6S2, CS2) by 14.0%-100%. 
Low-intensity aeration (2.3-3.5 mL/g(TS)/d) only transformed organic 
sulfides, whereas high-intensity aeration (≥9.3 mL/g(TS)/d) achieved 
complete removal of sulfur-containing compounds. Moreover, micro- 
aeration significantly enhanced methane production by 37.6%-95.5% 
compared with the control. However, elevated aeration intensity 
concurrently accelerated substrate carbon mineralization, as evidenced 
by an increase in dry matter loss from 19.0% in the control to 38.8% at 
the maximum aeration rate (13.9 mL/g(TS)/d). Furthermore, microbial 
analysis revealed that micro-aeration enriched facultative taxa (e.g., 
unclassified_f__Bacillaceae and Gammaproteobacteria) and up-regulated 
pathways related to sulfur oxidation, nitrogen fixation, fatty acid 
β-oxidation, and acetyl-CoA synthesis, promoting odor elimination. 
Moderate aeration (4.6 mL/g(TS)/d) enriched Syntrophomonas, Meth­
anothrix, and Methanosarcina, while enhancing sulfur oxidation and fatty 
acid conversion potentials that promoted methanogenesis. Overall, 
4.6 mL/g(TS)/d was identified as the optimal aeration intensity, 
achieving the balance between odor removal and methane production. 
These findings provide theoretical support and operational parameters 
for regulating anaerobic digestion of pig manure.
